CHAPTER 12: NOVEMBER 14

Grace was up at five-thirty. She filled the coffee pot, set it on the burner, and stood at the counter in the kitchen light while the house was still dark around her. November dark. The kind that pressed against the windows like it wanted in.

She made Dan's lunch the way she made it every morning. Tuna on white bread, the can opened and drained and mixed with mayonnaise and a little celery salt, the way her mother had made it for her father in this same kitchen when this had been her parents' house and the world had been a different shape. She spread the tuna with a butter knife, her hands moving without thought — hands that were forty-one years old and looked fifty, the knuckles swollen from hot water and fryer grease, the skin across the backs cracked in fine white lines like the glaze on old china. She wrapped the sandwich in wax paper, folded the edges tight, wrapped it again in aluminum foil. An apple. Two oatmeal cookies from Sunday night. Brown paper bag. Thermos.

Dan came down at six-fifteen. Work boots, jeans, flannel shirt. He poured coffee, drank half of it standing at the counter, set the mug in the sink.

"Let him sleep," he said, meaning Nick, who was upstairs in a seventeen-year-old's coma after staying up past midnight working through a chord progression in the garage. "He's got calculus first period."

107:He looked at the workbench. Dan's red metal toolbox sat where it always sat, heavy and scarred, the paint chipped at the corners. Nick had never opened it. You didn't open another man's toolbox the same way you didn't read another man's mail.
117:Under the sheet music, a spiral notebook. The cover was soft with handling, the wire binding bent from being shoved into the toolbox a hundred times. Nick opened it.
128:Not in public. Not in the garage when Nick was practicing, not anywhere his family could see. In the hours after Grace went to bed, in the early mornings before anyone was up, Dan had sat in this garage and played guitar and written songs and never told anyone. He'd hidden it the way some men hide drinking — not out of shame but out of the belief that the thing you love most is the thing you can least afford to need. He'd had a dream and he'd put it in a toolbox and closed the lid and gone to work.
146:Grace reached over and closed the toolbox lid. The latch clicked shut with a sound that was quiet and final.
148:She couldn't open it again. The toolbox would sit on the workbench for years, and Grace would clean around it and never touch it, because inside it was the version of Dan she hadn't been able to save.
150:Nick would open it again. Many times. He would take out the notebook and study his father's chord progressions and learn them by heart, and when he played them on his own guitar the notes would sound like inheritance — not money, not property, not the things that pass from father to son in families that have things to pass. Something that couldn't be delayed for cost savings or dropped from thirty-one stories or sealed in a closed casket.

def find_chapter_range(lines, ch_num, next_markers):
    """Return (start_idx, end_idx_exclusive) for a chapter header block."""
    start = None
    for i, ln in enumerate(lines):
        if re.match(rf"^(# |## )?CHAPTER {ch_num}(:|$|\s)", ln.strip()) and not re.match(rf"^(# |## )?CHAPTER {ch_num}[A-Z]", ln.strip()):

    if start is None:

    end = len(lines)
    for j in range(start+1, len(lines)):
        s = lines[j].strip()
        if re.match(r"^(# |## )?CHAPTER \d+[A-Z]?(:|$|\s)", s):
            end = j

    return start, end

CHAPTER 23A: PATTY'S DECISION

The rooster didn't crow at the Lally place. The pigs handled that — two hundred and sixty Yorkshires grunting their way to consciousness at five-fifteen every morning, a sound like the earth clearing its throat.

Patty Lally pulled on her boots at the back door and stepped into April air thick with the smell of hog waste and wet hay. The southeast corner of Sudbury didn't wake up pretty. It woke up honest.

She'd done morning feed since she was twelve. Five-gallon buckets of grain mixed with kitchen scraps, distributed across eight pens while her father checked water lines and her mother tallied receipts at the kitchen table. The pigs pressed against the gates when they saw her coming — not affection, just hunger wearing a familiar face. Patty didn't mind. There was something clean about a relationship that never pretended to be more than it was.

The Cavicchio farm sprawled three fields east, and when the wind came from that direction the combined stench of two pig operations could stop traffic on Landham Road. People on the west side of Hop Brook called it the smell of Southeast. They meant it as an insult. Patty wore it like a badge.

# ACT II

---


CHAPTER 13: MAXANNE — WHEN FRIENDSHIP STARTED DYING

Three hours left.

The demo cassette is on the console at my right hand. Maxell, ninety-minute, label hand-printed in ballpoint: *Demo — Nick/Jackie — un-Authorized — March 1979*. The plastic's warm. I keep picking it up and putting it down like I'm trying to decide if it's real.

The ON AIR sign blinks. Behind the glass, the kid they gave me for engineering — Bruins hoodie, laptop open, Red Bull sweating on the table — thinks music starts when somebody opens a DAW. He doesn't know he's working my last shift. They drew straws for tonight and I drew short. Everybody else gave their speeches this week. What you're hearing now is the one nobody wanted.
==END Ch13 / START Ch14==

Stay with me.

**END CHAPTER 13**


CHAPTER 14: THE BRIDGE WHERE FRIENDSHIP DIED

The second Saturday in October, 1978. Eleven months since the trailer on the Pru, near enough to a year that Nick had stopped counting and started rounding. The woods between Dutton Road and Cavicchio's back field were conservation land now, and the old stone walls ran through them waist-high, moss-headed, the farmers who'd stacked them a century gone and the sheep gone longer than that.

Nick led on the CR125. He'd rebuilt it over two summers out of scrap Dan had let him haul home from the dump — a '72 frame, a '74 engine set in one August Saturday with a jack and a two-by-four, which was how you did it if you were Dan and his son. The pull-start took three today before the plug cleared. The bark of the two-stroke came up through his wrist thin at idle, angry at half-throttle, the pre-mix sweet in the cold air. The grips had worn smooth to the shape of his hands. The handguards were Cavicchio-mud, spring-brown, because Nick didn't wash a bike for weather he'd just put back in the weather.

The trail was their runway. You rode it because you owned it, and you owned it because nobody else wanted it, and you didn't own much else.
==END Ch18 / START Ch18A==

Grace set the receiver back in the cradle of the rotary phone on the kitchen wall, and the small internal click of the hanger-bar dropping into place was the last sound in the house. The kitchen clock ticked. Upstairs the garage amp was off. She stood with her hand still on the receiver for a second, then she turned off the kitchen light and went up the stairs in the dark the way she had gone up them ten thousand times, her right hand on the banister where the varnish had worn thin to the grain under her father's hand and her own.

**END CHAPTER 18**


CHAPTER 18A: THE STATION MEETING

Two hours and forty-one minutes.

Grace Johnson just left a PTA meeting in her Friendly's uniform and told a room full of professionals what they didn't want to hear. Forty-two to eleven. Not even close. I told you that woman had steel in her spine.

I pour another inch of Pappy. Just an inch. I need to be sharp enough to finish this story and drunk enough to tell the truth.
==END Ch23 / START Ch23A==

Stay with me.

**END CHAPTER 23**


CHAPTER 23A: PATTY'S DECISION

---

The rooster didn't crow at the Lally place. The pigs handled that — two hundred and sixty Yorkshires grunting their way to consciousness at five-fifteen every morning, a sound like the earth clearing its throat.

Patty Lally pulled on her boots at the back door and stepped into April air thick with the smell of hog waste and wet hay. The southeast corner of Sudbury didn't wake up pretty. It woke up honest.

CHAPTER 24: PATTY RETURNS

May 14th, 1979. St. Michael's, Sudbury, a little after nine. The last car door in the parking lot had been Steve's Chevette — the driver-side hinge whining past halfway — and Patty had counted it the way she counted beats, and then she'd been alone.

Rumours had packed up an hour ago: Kristy's amp, Robin's kick pedal, Steve's snare in its padded bag. They'd hugged her at the parish-hall door the way you hug somebody the night before surgery, a little too long and too careful, and now the sanctuary was what it always was on a Monday night, which was empty.

She had moved the guitar in here on purpose. The acoustic was a hand-me-down from her uncle in Hudson, a Yamaha FG-180 with a scratch along the lower bout where somebody at some wedding had set down a beer bottle. It lived in a soft case with a broken zipper she held shut with a shoelace.
==END Ch25 / START Ch26==
---

The Lincoln-Sudbury parking lot lay empty under its one sodium lamp, the stage door locked, the gym dark. A freight train pulled east toward Boston along the Route 20 cut, and the night closed behind it.

**END CHAPTER 25**


# CHAPTER 26: THE BATTLE BEGINS

May 15th, 1979. Seven o'clock on a Tuesday night, and the Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium was filling up with kids who'd been told this mattered.

Grace Johnson had changed at home before leaving, putting on her best dress—the one she'd worn to church and Dan's funeral and the middle school talent show when Nick won. She'd taken off early from her shift at Friendly's to see her son play tonight.

CHAPTER 21: NICK'S REHEARSAL

The garage bay door stood up to the chest-high stop, lifted halfway for the air — May eighth in Sudbury, sixty-five degrees if it was a degree, the kind of spring night that felt warm only because April had set the bar so low. Crickets had started in the grass by the oil stain. Behind the Cavicchio fence a spring peeper was going in the wet low place, one note at a time, not fast. A Chevy with a bad belt whined down Dutton Road and faded toward the Horse Pond light.

Inside the garage the air was forty watts worse than outside. One bare bulb on a length of exposed Romex swung a finger's width when a kid walked under it. The Marshall practice amp on the milk crate was warm enough to put a palm on. The guitar case was open on the concrete, cables heaped in it like rope in a dinghy.

Nick stood in the middle of it with the twenty-five-dollar acoustic he'd walked out of a pawn shop in Framingham with the summer he was fourteen — four springs ago, Dan still around for one more year, the price Dan had paid because he'd said *don't tell your mother* and then told her at dinner that night himself. The guitar had a crack in the upper bout Nick had packed with wood glue the summer he was fifteen. His fingertips knew every raised grain on the neck.
==END Ch22 / START Ch23==

He took off his shoes, set them at the foot of the bed, and got under the covers in his clothes.

**END CHAPTER 22**


CHAPTER 23: MAXANNE — THE EVE OF BATTLE

Three hours into the broadcast. One hour left.

The Heaven Hill paper cup has gone soft at the rim. I refill it. My hands on the console are steady now. Guilt doesn't shake you forever. It just sits down beside you and waits for the cue.

The ON AIR sign holds its red like an open wound. Behind the glass, the kid finally put the phone down. Quit scrolling about an hour ago. He's watching me the way you watch an old drunk at a bar who's about to say something true.
==END Ch21==
Nick set the guitar down in the case on the tangle of cables. He closed the lid. He did not latch it. He reached up and pulled the bay door down to the concrete with both hands, slow, the way Dan had taught him, easing the springs the last six inches so the counterweight did not slam.

On his way to the side door he did not look at the toolbox.

**END CHAPTER 21**


CHAPTER 22: JACKIE'S REHEARSAL

May 14, 1979. Early evening. Eighteen hours to the Battle and Jackie Marsh was alone in the basement on Maple Street, running the intro of "Bohemian Rhapsody" in B-flat because his left hand had asked for it the second he sat down.

The room had been finished the summer he turned fourteen. Foam panels on the walls, the two-inch studio kind — white once, now going yellow at the glued edges the way a paperback goes yellow on a south-facing shelf. A Shure SM58 stood on a boom stand at the center of the floor, black grille, the XLR running in a clean loop to the four-track against the wall — a Tascam, four little red LED indicators glowing dim as pilot lights in a kitchen at night. Against the long wall, the upright. A 1920s Baldwin, its walnut case gone plum-dark at the corners, its ivory top keys chipped in two places from a thumbnail that had been Eileen's mother's in 1931 in a parlor on Beacon Hill. The Steinway lived upstairs in the good light. The Baldwin lived down here with the amps. That had been decided early.

## CHAPTER 28: NICK'S PERFORMANCE

### **Walking the Line (9:00 PM)**

And then it was time for Walking the Line.

Nick Johnson walked onto the stage carrying his pawn shop guitar with hands that showed calluses from more than just playing music. He wore his best jeans—which meant his least-torn jeans—and a black t-shirt that said nothing because it didn't need to. No costume, no pretense, no attempt to be anything other than exactly what he was: a seventeen-year-old boy from the wrong side of Hop Brook who'd been chosen to prove that talent didn't require a trust fund.

Behind him, Stephen Murphy took his position at the drums, his face serious with concentration. Tommy Morrison picked up his bass guitar, and Danny Kowalski settled behind the keyboard. They were Walking the Line, and they were about to prove that authenticity could be just as powerful as technical excellence.

Nick looked out at the audience, at the northeast section where his natural constituency sat, at the southwest section where Jackie's people applauded polish over passion. He saw Grace Johnson in the front row, her face a study in controlled pride, watching her son transform disadvantage into art.

And then he began to play.

### **"Walk This Way"**

The opening riff of "Walk This Way" filled the auditorium like a declaration of war. Nick's guitar was raw, unpolished, authentic in a way that made you believe every note was being played for the first time. This wasn't just an Aerosmith cover—this was Aerosmith distilled, purified, made real without losing its rock and roll soul.
---

She stood for a minute in the wing with her boots in her hand and listened to the applause do what applause did when it was not going to stop on its own, which was go on until somebody on the crew brought the house lights up the rest of the way.

**END CHAPTER 29**


## CHAPTER 29: PATTY'S PERFORMANCE

### **Rumours (8:40 PM)**

There are nights when one song can shift the fault lines of a whole town—and then there are nights like this one, when it takes a girl with a secondhand guitar and a voice pitched somewhere between a force of nature and a gentle plea.

Patty Lally hadn’t grown up in Sudbury, but as she took the stage, barefoot on the dark riser, it didn’t matter where she called home. Her hair was loose, honey in the high school lights. She looked smaller than the others who’d come before—until she set her guitar’s shoulder strap and found the microphone. Then, all at once, she was the axis of the room.

No one expected strategy from Patty. No one expected revolution. They expected Fleetwood Mac covers and a nice voice, maybe something to fill the time until the next big act. Even Nick and Jackie, cooling their nerves in the wings, figured they knew how this set would go.

CHAPTER 29: PATTY'S PERFORMANCE

Patty kicked her boots off stage-right and stepped onto the riser barefoot. The stage wood was warm where the lights had been cooking it for two hours. Nick's band had left a smell behind — sweat and amp dust and the faint burnt-resistor tang of a Marshall that had been run hard — and under that, because she carried it with her, there was the faint sour-sweet smell of pig on her flannel, which she knew, and was not going to apologize for to a room of nine hundred and eighty-five people.

She set the Yamaha on its strap. The scratch along the lower bout caught the gel light the blue of a bruise. The soft case lay open behind her amp, the shoelace she tied it shut with trailing out over the edge of the riser.

Robin came up on her left with the bass. Kristy took the Fender and the second mic. Steve Bankuti was already behind the kit, a kid from Sudbury Southeast whose father drove a milk route; he adjusted his snare stand one quarter-turn and then sat with his sticks crossed on his knee like a boy waiting to be told he was allowed to stand up at the dinner table.

Patty leaned into the mic. She did not say anything. She tuned her B string — B was always the one — and she nodded at Robin.

In the wings stage-left Nick was leaning on a flight case with a towel around his neck. In the wings stage-right, across the width of the proscenium, Jackie was standing the way Jackie stood when he was trying not to be seen, hands at his sides, the black piano jacket still buttoned. Patty saw both of them the way you see a thing you are not going to look at twice. She looked back at the neck of the guitar.

Steve's kick pedal squeaked on beat two. A small high squeak, a dry hinge, the way his father's truck door squeaked. Patty smiled — a small unmeant smile, because something had surprised her — and went into the opening figure of "Dreams."

*Now here you go again, you say you want your freedom.*
---
She stood for a minute in the wing with her boots in her hand and listened to the applause do what applause did when it was not going to stop on its own, which was go on until somebody on the crew brought the house lights up the rest of the way.

**END CHAPTER 29**



CHAPTER 30
THE ANNOUNCEMENT

The judges' room smelled like burned coffee and indecision.

Four folding chairs around a cafeteria table. Fluorescent lights that turned everyone the color of old newspaper. Maxanne Sartori sat with her back to the door, her fingers wrapped around a Styrofoam cup she hadn't drunk from in twenty minutes. Across from her, Carter Alan leaned forward on his elbows, jaw working like he was chewing something that wouldn't break down. Chuck Morrison had his legal pad covered in notes he kept crossing out. Bob Walker stood at the window, watching the parking lot fill with headlights as families arrived for the announcement.

"We've been at this forty minutes," Carter said.

"I'm aware." Maxanne set down the cup. A ring of coffee bloomed on the table beneath it.

41:"Corporate picked this song because it sounds like grief without committing to any. Because it's long enough to run out the clock. Because the Christian broadcasting people taking this frequency at one minute past midnight needed something that would end the old story quietly so the new story could begin. And I will say this, because I have to say it on the air before I do anything else tonight — corporate got it right. Accidentally. For the first time in thirty years of corporate getting everything wrong, somebody in North Carolina picked the correct song for a rock station going dark. Syd Barrett deserves it. Pink Floyd deserves it. The people who spent fifty-six years listening to this frequency deserve it. 'Shine On' is the elegy. I mean that. I'm ready to play it."
119:The hallway's moving boxes have not moved. The lobby is darker than when I came in. Outside, August in Boston, asphalt and harbor, the antenna tower dark against the sky for the first time in fifty-six years.

19:The lobby is a labyrinth of cardboard.
119:I can say that to myself and mean it. The corporate overlords accidentally wrote the right song. "Shine On You Crazy Diamond" is a real elegy — twenty-six minutes of Gilmour's guitar reaching for a man who wasn't coming back, saxophone in the middle like a funeral procession, Gilmour's voice finally breaking on *you reached for the secret too soon, you cried for the moon*. That's what you play when a rock and roll station dies. Not a demo tape with a hairline crack down the shell. Not two kids from Sudbury nobody knows. Not a private grudge against a labyrinth I helped build.

Somewhere in a practice room on Mass Ave, on a Wednesday afternoon a month from now, a man in his late forties will be sitting at a Steinway Model B teaching an undergraduate about voice leading. Someone will come to the door with a laptop. Somebody will say, you have to hear this. He will not move at first. He will listen all the way through, four minutes and forty-three seconds, with his hands in his lap and his eyes closed. And when it ends he will lift his hands and put them on the keys, and he will play the D minor chord, just the chord, just once — and he will nod, very slightly, the way people nod when they finally hear somebody say out loud the thing they had decided they were alone with.

That's enough. That's what the tape is for. That's what the frequency was for, all along.

The reel turns, somewhere, in some kid's bedroom in Quincy, in some apartment in Somerville, in some dorm in Ann Arbor, in some kitchen in Manchester, New Hampshire, at one-twenty in the morning on August twelfth, two thousand and nine. Two boys in a room that no longer exists are still playing. The harmony found its receivers.

I turn the key. The Volvo catches on the second try. I drive out onto the Pike heading west, toward Cambridge, toward home, and I leave the radio off.

I sat in the judge's panel between two other WBCN DJs, clipboard in hand, trying to look professional while watching something die in real time.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_Complete.txt:2433:I watched their friendship continue to drown in front of 985 witnesses. Public execution disguised as competition. And I'd sold the tickets.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_Complete.txt:2704:Inside, the auditorium filled with eight hundred people—high school kids, parents, friends, siblings who'd come to see their brothers or sisters play. The Rampers claimed the front rows, their usual territory. The Rats took up positions along the back and aisles, boots up on seats. The Regs settled into the middle sections, trying to stay invisible. The Rollers were scattered throughout, like they'd forgotten there was supposed to be a system.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_Complete.txt:2801:Jackie stood up, his legs feeling foreign beneath him. He walked to the edge of the stage, peered through the curtain, looked out at the 800 people who'd come to see eight bands compete for a prize that didn't matter and a title that meant less. He saw his father in the front row, Dr. Richard Marsh sitting with perfect posture, his face a study in controlled pride. Jackie would either prove tonight that his father's investment had been worth it, or he would finally expose the doubt that had been eating him alive for months.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_Complete.txt:2865:But now, on this stage, surrounded by 800 people who expected him to prove something, Jackie understood that he wasn't singing about needing somebody else to love him. He was singing about needing to love himself, about needing to stop choosing between classical approval and rock breath, about needing to be enough for himself instead of for anyone else.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_1_Complete.txt:3511:May 15, 1979. Seven o'clock on a Tuesday night. The Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium had been built in 1958 and smelled like it still — wood floor wax, the slow mineral breath of cast iron, nine hundred and eighty-five folding seats bolted into a concrete rake that groaned as kids sat down and groaned again when kids stood back up to wave at other kids. The fluorescent cove lights above the proscenium threw the whole room into the color of a grocery store. Behind the stage hung the painted backdrop every school play had used for a decade: a Concord Road maple tree in October, the red gone brown at the edges where the scrim had rolled. In the lobby the JV booster club had set up a popcorn machine and the smell of commercial butter and Aqua Velva and girls' perfume had come in with the crowd and was now layered, impossibly, on top of the baseline adolescent sweat of an April-warm room in May. The balcony was already full. Seniors.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_1_Complete.txt:3671:Nick had been watching the gap between the curtain and the proscenium wall — a slice of stage, the back of Jackie's head at the piano — running the set in his head the way a guy runs a road before he drives it. Then Jackie hit the note in *Somebody to Love* and the note did not come out the way eleven years of lessons had built it to come out. It cracked. The auditorium did the thing eight hundred and fifty people do when they are holding one breath together — a half-second where nobody coughed.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_1_Complete.txt:3747:She was looking at him and she was not looking away. Across eight hundred and fifty people he held her there for the length of the solo's pickup bar. If he held her any longer he would not finish the song. He looked back down at the fretboard.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_1_Complete.txt:3778:Patty kicked her boots off stage-right and stepped onto the riser barefoot. The stage wood was warm where the lights had been cooking it for two hours. Nick's band had left a smell behind — sweat and amp dust and the faint burnt-resistor tang of a Marshall that had been run hard — and under that, because she carried it with her, there was the faint sour-sweet smell of pig on her flannel, which she knew, and was not going to apologize for to a room of nine hundred and eighty-five people.
Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_1_Complete.txt:3808:The hum had been in her for seven months. It had caught on her flute G key in Mr. Wentworth's room with Nick's amp plugged in and Jackie's hands on the keys. It had caught in her throat on the eve, a splinter in a finger, a sow sighing out in the dark barn. It had sat folded with the seven letters in the back of the camp notebook. Now it came all the way out. Not a fragment. Not a hum. The whole song, at full voice, in front of nine hundred and eighty-five people, her bare feet on a warm stage, the Yamaha FG-180 hanging off her shoulder by a hand-me-down strap.

55:"Jackie Marsh lived less than a mile away as the crow flies, but between them stretched Hop Brook—named a century ago for its hops, the old mill long gone to modernization. The brook divided Sudbury like a scar, separating the haves from the have-nots. In winter, kids from both sides skated the same nearby pond trying to emulate Bobby Orr's graceful glides across the ice, but when the ice melted, they returned to their proper territories. Jackie's father a Trauma Psychiatrist and a professor at Boston University.  A social climber.  He published papers about childhood trauma and yet was ignorant to what actually evolved around him.
67:"This tape I am holding is the only recording that exists of Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh playing together. The shred of evidence that we chose division over music. The rest of the story? That's what the next four hours are for. So pour yourself something strong, turn off your IPhone, and let me tell you how the Battle of the Bands became a war and about "The Band That Never Was."
90:She studied Maxanne—bell-bottoms, oversized sunglasses, standing on the cracked front step like a visitor from a planet where people bought clothes that didn't come from the Jordan Marsh clearance rack.
151:Jackie Marsh woke at 6:47 AM—three minutes before his alarm, the way he always did. His bedroom was the kind of perfect that only happened when adults designed spaces for children they wanted to be proud of. The walls were painted a color his mother called "Dove Gray," the bookshelves held alphabetized volumes he'd actually read, and his piano sat in the corner like a judge waiting to render verdict.
159:Tonight was the recital. Tonight, he would sit in front of his parents' friends and his father's colleagues and play Chopin and Bach and Debussy like he'd been trained to do since he was five years old. Tonight, everyone would applaud politely and tell Dr. Marsh that his son was remarkably talented, and Dr. Marsh would accept the compliments like tributes to his excellent parenting.
167:The same week Maxanne Sartori discovered Nick Johnson's garage, Dr. Richard Marsh had called the station personally—a rare gesture, since university professors usually delegated such tasks to their secretaries. But Dr. Marsh wanted to ensure Maxanne understood just how significant his son's recital would be.
171:Maxanne had wanted to decline. Classical recitals were not her beat. But something in Dr. Marsh's voice—a father's pride laced with something else, almost fear—compelled her to agree. Maybe it was recognizing that same desperation she'd heard in Grace Johnson's "don't fill his head with dreams we can't afford." Different words, same underlying terror that music might ruin a child's future.
175:By seven o'clock that evening, the Marsh house stood transformed. The living room had become a concert space—folding chairs in perfect rows, a rented Steinway grand piano that cost more than Grace Johnson made in a year, champagne chilling in silver buckets for the afterward. The audience was prep school parents and university faculty, the kind of people who applauded with their fingertips and discussed summer houses on the Cape between selections.
177:The Marsh house stood on the good side of Hop Brook like it had been placed there by a decorator: Colonial perfection, black shutters against white clapboard, a lawn that would be green come spring. You could walk from Nick Johnson's garage to this front door in twelve minutes, but you'd have to cross Hop Brook—and that narrow stream might as well have been the Atlantic.
185:Jackie Marsh entered the living room at precisely 7:30 PM in a tuxedo that had been tailored to fit him perfectly, seventeen years old but carrying himself like someone who'd been preparing for this moment since birth. He was beautiful in that way that good nutrition and orthodontics and SAT tutors can manufacture. But when he sat at the piano, something changed.
191:The audience nodded appreciatively, already composing the compliments they'd deliver with their champagne. Dr. Marsh sat in the front row, his expression carefully neutral but his posture radiating satisfaction. This was exactly what he'd paid for.
197:Between the Rachmaninoff and the final Mozart, Jackie paused. The pause stretched longer than it should have. Dr. Marsh cleared his throat—a warning about maintaining proper recital pacing. But Jackie wasn't listening to his father. He was listening to something else.
207:He sang. His voice, trained for Schubert lieder and careful projection, broke open. The champagne glasses on the sideboard vibrated. Dr. Marsh's water glass hummed against its coaster. Four minutes and fifty-five seconds, and Jackie Marsh wasn't performing for anyone in that room.
211:Dr. Marsh was the first to speak. "That was... unexpected."
221:Jackie took the card. His hands were still shaking. He looked at it, then at Maxanne, then at his father's face — which had rearranged itself into something Jackie had never seen before. Not anger. Not pride. Something older and more complicated, like a man watching his son make a choice he recognized from his own youth. Dr. Marsh's right hand moved to his left wrist and pressed there — an unconscious gesture, the place where calluses had once formed on fingers that used to grip a guitar neck, years before economics replaced music and security replaced risk.
225:The other guests murmured. Mrs. Marsh moved through the room offering champagne, deflecting questions, doing what she'd been trained to do when the social order cracked.
282:Jackie Marsh sat alone at the corner table closest to the emergency exit. He held a carton of milk that had been sitting out long enough to feel like bathwater against his palm. His brown hair was cut short above the ears—his mother's instructions to the barber, not his—and his polo shirt was tucked in, pressed, creased along the sleeves like someone had ironed it that morning. Someone had. His sneakers were white. Not dirty-white, not scuffed-white. White-white. The kind of white that announced to every kid in the cafeteria that this boy had not yet been allowed to discover the outdoors.
350:Jackie took the hand. His own fingers were clean, the nails trimmed straight across. "Jackie Marsh. We just moved here from Ithaca."
434:The first time Jackie came to dinner at the Johnson house, Grace watched him from the kitchen doorway. She'd heard about the Marsh family from the other mothers — the psychiatrist at Boston University, the house on Concord Road, the kind of people who didn't usually sit at tables with mismatched chairs and bills spread on the counter.
446:"Jackie Marsh," Jackie said, standing up and extending his hand.
552:The thermostat in the Marsh dining room was set to sixty-eight degrees. Always sixty-eight degrees. CHAPTER 11A

April in Sudbury was all mud. Hop Brook ran brown under the Route 117 bridge, loud enough to hear from the Lincoln-Sudbury front walk, and the lawn in front of the school had gone to the color of a boot print that had filled with water and frozen and thawed a dozen times since March. The parking lot was a lattice of tire ruts. A kid came up the walk, stepped wrong, went in past the ankle of his sneaker, said a word his mother wouldn't like, pulled his foot out with a sucking sound, and kept walking. Nobody looked. April.

Seven-forty-five. First bell in four.

Carl Marquis's '66 Impala came in off Lincoln Road from the south, throwing gravel, the muffler louder than it had been yesterday. Nick was in the passenger seat, book bag between his feet, a quarter-eaten Hostess donut in his hand, his hair still wet from the shower he'd taken at six-thirty. The radio was on an AM station playing something neither good nor bad — noise to fill the seven miles from Marquis's driveway to the school lot. The speaker in the driver's door buzzed on the high notes. It had buzzed since Carl and his father put the dash back together in November. It was just the sound the car made now.

Nick got out. He slammed the door the way you slammed the door of a car like that — a second slam, because the first one never caught.

Up the walk, twenty yards away, a wood-paneled Buick Estate wagon pulled up to the curb. The wagon was always clean. Dr. Richard Marsh had Saturday-morning habits about wax and a chamois, and it showed. Jackie got out of the passenger side, closed the door with the small respectful click a kid closed a clean car with, and lifted his hand once to the driver's-side window without looking at his father's face. The Buick pulled away. Jackie stood on the curb a beat longer than he had to, adjusting the strap of his book bag, then moved up the walk.

His loafers were polished. The bottoms of his jeans were an inch dark with Dutton Road mud because he had walked across the lawn yesterday to save thirty seconds. He noticed it now, the small pull of dried mud against the denim at every step.

Nick was fifteen yards to his left, coming in from the parking lot at a diagonal. Nick saw him. His eyes went to Jackie the way a dog's head turned when another dog walked by — before the thinking got there. Then Nick looked down at his own boots, at the donut in his hand, at the cigarette butt somebody had ground out in the gravel by his toe, and kept walking. His line and Jackie's line converged toward the same set of double doors and stopped converging eight feet before the doors, because Jackie went toward the right-hand door and Nick went toward the left, and they passed through at the same moment through doors hinged at different walls, and neither one looked at the other, and then they were inside and the hallway noise took them and they went in separate directions without a sentence between them.

The bell rang. In the window of the front office, a secretary picked up a rotary phone and began to dial.

---

...

In booth four, the Carvajal family — mother, father, two kids under ten, a baby in a plastic carrier on the bench — was eating Happy Endings sundaes and arguing gently about who had gotten the extra cherry. The father worked at Raytheon on Hartwell. The kids had Fribble mustaches. Grace had brought them their check five minutes ago and would bring them a handful of the little red-wrapped mints with the coffee if the father ordered coffee, which he would.

Grace moved along the counter. Refilled Bellenghi. Refilled Rossi. Smiled at the Carvajal kids — the smile that had one specific watt for children and another for adults and a third for drunks coming in off the Post Road at eleven — and slid a clean glass of water in front of Donna Koslowski and took the empty and said *you let me know when you want another* and Donna said *Grace you are a saint* and Grace said *not yet* and kept moving.

At the end of the counter, below the register, she bent to pull a fresh stack of green guest checks out of the cardboard box on the shelf. Her knees made a small sound she ignored because she had been ignoring it since March. She came back up and set the stack in the apron pocket on top of the old stack. She had a pen in her hand already. She did not know she had picked it up.

Through the plate-glass window, across the lot, a station wagon pulled into a space under the lamp post and a family of four got out — father, mother, a boy and a girl, no one Grace knew — and walked toward the door in that slow family formation that meant they had already decided what they were ordering on the drive over. Grace watched them for the length of a breath, without thinking about them, without thinking at all. Then in the booth the Carvajal father lifted his hand for coffee and Grace was already moving toward the pot, and the pencil behind her ear stayed where it was, and the green checks in her apron pocket shifted against her hip as she walked.

**END CHAPTER 11A**

CHAPTER 12: NOVEMBER 14

Grace was up at five-thirty. She filled the coffee pot, set it on the burner, and stood at the counter in the kitchen light while the house was still dark around her. November dark. The kind that pressed against the windows like it wanted in.

She made Dan's lunch the way she made it every morning. Tuna on white bread, the can opened and drained and mixed with mayonnaise and a little celery salt, the way her mother had made it for her father in this same kitchen when this had been her parents' house and the world had been a different shape. She spread the tuna with a butter knife, her hands moving without thought — hands that were forty-one years old and looked fifty, the knuckles swollen from hot water and fryer grease, the skin across the backs cracked in fine white lines like the glaze on old china. She wrapped the sandwich in wax paper, folded the edges tight, wrapped it again in aluminum foil. An apple. Two oatmeal cookies from Sunday night. Brown paper bag. Thermos.

Dan came down at six-fifteen. Work boots, jeans, flannel shirt. He poured coffee, drank half of it standing at the counter, set the mug in the sink.

    end = len(lines)

I wrote them that night.

Alone in my apartment in Brookline — a one-bedroom with a fire escape that rattled when trucks passed and a kitchen window that looked out on a brick wall close enough to touch. I sat at my kitchen table with a legal pad and a bottle of red wine and wrote the rules for WBCN's first Battle of the Bands like I was drafting a treaty between two countries that didn't know they were at war.

Entry requirements. Judging criteria — originality, emotional connection, technical ability, stage presence, with originality and emotional connection weighted double. Prize structure — five hundred dollars to the winner, and a recording session at WBCN's Studio C for the winner and any runner-up.

And then I got to Article 7, Section 3.

I poured more wine.

Article 7, Section 3: "In the event of a tie in the final round, all tied contestants shall share the studio recording session equally, collaborating on material of their choosing, to demonstrate the spirit of musical cooperation that WBCN's Battle of the Bands is designed to foster."

I read it back. The language was clean, legal, boring. The kind of clause nobody reads in a rules packet. Boilerplate. Standard contest legalese.

Except it wasn't.

I'd already heard the rumors. Two kids from Sudbury — one working-class, one wealthy, once best friends, now enemies — both entering the Battle. Nick Johnson, the guitar kid from Dutton Road with the dead father's garage and the sound that could pull tears out of people who didn't know they were sad. Jackie Marsh, the classically trained prodigy from Maple Street with the Queen belt buckle and the rock and roll heart trapped inside a Juilliard application.

I'd already visited both of them. Already heard what they could do separately. Already imagined — the way you imagine a song before you write it, hearing the ghost of the melody before a single note is played — what they could do together.

The tie clause wasn't boilerplate. It was an ambush. A carefully engineered piece of fine print designed to force two estranged friends into the same recording studio, because I'd convinced myself that if they just played together one more time, they'd remember. They'd hear the frequency they'd lost. They'd find their way back to the harmony that had made a middle school gymnasium stand on its feet four years earlier.

I was engineering reconciliation the way Kowalski engineered demographics. Using rules and structures to produce an outcome I'd already decided was right. Convinced that because my intentions were good — because I genuinely wanted those boys to make music together — the manipulation was justified. Noble, even.

I finished the wine. Slid the legal pad across the table and stared at Article 7, Section 3.

"It's just a contingency," I said to my empty kitchen. "Standard contest procedure. Ties happen."

Ties happen. Right. And lightning happens, and asteroids happen, and sometimes the thing you've been hoping for your entire career just falls into your lap. Except this wasn't going to fall. I was going to push it. I was going to score those boys close enough that the tie clause would trigger, and then I was going to put them in a room and lock the door and call it opportunity.

Because I believed — genuinely, desperately, with every molecule of the woman who'd walked into the Brickyard in 1973 and heard a sound that changed her life — that Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh belonged together. That their separation was a crime against music. That if the world wasn't going to fix this, Maxanne Sartori would.

I turned off the kitchen light. Went to bed. Slept the kind of sleep you only get when you've told yourself a lie you really need to believe.

---

2009. Studio B. My hands around the demo tape.

"That was the meeting," I say into the microphone. "April 1979. The day WBCN officially became a business instead of a movement. The day I watched a man with demographic charts convince a room full of rebels that rebellion could be monetized, and the rebels — the rebels meaning me — said yes because we thought we could outrun the cage."

I turn the tape in my hands. The label in my block lettering. Evidence.

"And that night, alone in my kitchen, I wrote the trap. Dressed it up as a contest rule. Told myself it was boilerplate when it was a loaded gun. I wrote Article 7, Section 3 knowing exactly what I was doing, and I lied to myself about it the way people always lie to themselves when they believe the ends justify the means."

The ON AIR light pulses. The station hums its late-night hum, the machinery of broadcast holding steady even as the clock eats what's left.

"Here's what I've learned in thirty years of carrying this around: the noble lie is the most dangerous kind. You can forgive a con artist — at least they know what they are. You can forgive a fool — at least they didn't mean it. But the person who manipulates you for your own good, who rigs the game because they're sure they know better, who writes the rules of your life in fine print and calls it opportunity — that person is the hardest to forgive. Because that person is convinced they love you."

I set the tape down.

"That was the moment I became what I'd fought. I just didn't know it yet. It would take two boys, a recording session, and thirty years of midnight silence for me to hear the frequency I'd jammed."

I cue the next track. "Somebody to Love." Queen. Freddie Mercury searching for what we all search for: someone who sees us as we are and doesn't look away.

"Three weeks until the Battle of the Bands. Nick Johnson is rehearsing in his dead father's garage. Jackie Marsh is rehearsing in his living father's basement. And I'm sitting in a radio station in Boston, holding a set of contest rules that are going to change everything."

I press play. Freddie's voice fills the booth — pleading, soaring, desperate for connection in a world that keeps handing him perfection when all he wants is something real.

"Get some sleep," Mary said.

"You too."

Grace set the receiver back in the cradle of the rotary phone on the kitchen wall, and the small internal click of the hanger-bar dropping into place was the last sound in the house. The kitchen clock ticked. Upstairs the garage amp was off. She stood with her hand still on the receiver for a second, then she turned off the kitchen light and went up the stairs in the dark the way she had gone up them ten thousand times, her right hand on the banister where the varnish had worn thin to the grain under her father's hand and her own.

**END CHAPTER 18**


CHAPTER 18A: THE STATION MEETING

Two hours and forty-one minutes.

Grace Johnson just left a PTA meeting in her Friendly's uniform and told a room full of professionals what they didn't want to hear. Forty-two to eleven. Not even close. I told you that woman had steel in her spine.

I pour another inch of Pappy. Just an inch. I need to be sharp enough to finish this story and drunk enough to tell the truth.

"You know what the difference is between a rebel and a sellout?" I say into the microphone. "About one meeting. One conference room. One moment when you trade what you believe for what they'll approve. That's all it takes. You walk in pure and walk out with a company line, and it happens so smooth you don't feel the cut until you're bleeding all over someone else's floor."

I lean back and the chair protests, and I think: I know how it feels.

"April 1979. Three weeks before the Battle of the Bands. Two months before the last gasp of everything WBCN was supposed to be. Let me tell you about the meeting that changed everything."

---

WBCN's management office sat on the third floor above the studios — a room that had once been somebody's idea of cool and had aged into somebody's idea of a health code violation. The carpet was the color of a bruise, stained with decades of spilled coffee and dropped cigarette ash. The walls held framed gold records from bands the station had broken, hung at angles that suggested whoever mounted them had been in a hurry or half in the bag. Aerosmith. J. Geils. Boston. The Cars. Each frame a trophy case for a war we'd already won and were about to surrender.

The conference table was a slab of pressboard that buckled in the middle, covered in ring stains from mugs that had been set down and picked up by ten years of people debating what rock and roll owed to its audience. I'd sat at this table when we decided to give Aerosmith their first heavy rotation. I'd sat here when we broke The Cars and the phones rang for three days straight. I'd argued at this table, cursed at this table, once threw a promotional ashtray at Tom Andrews across this table because he wanted to put a jingle between Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath.

This table was where the real work happened. And now it was where the real work was going to die.

The meeting started at ten AM. Charlie Morris — station manager, joint-smoker, believer in the power of letting DJs run free — sat at the head, which told me nothing was wrong. But the man sitting to Charlie's right told me everything was wrong.

His name was Gerald Kowalski. New Program Director, hired six weeks earlier from a station in New York City. Late thirties, sharp jaw, hair parted with the mathematical precision of someone who'd never in his life played an instrument or felt the floor shake under a Marshall stack. He wore a suit in a building where nobody wore suits. He carried a leather portfolio the color of money. His shoes were Italian and polished to a shine that reflected the overhead fluorescents like a funhouse mirror.

I hated him on sight, which I understand isn't fair. But I've spent my life trusting my instincts about people the same way I trust them about music, and Gerald Kowalski's frequency was static. Pure, manufactured, corporate static.

Tom Andrews sat across from me. Tom — who'd been at WBCN since '71, who'd broken J. Geils when Peter Wolf was still his overnight DJ roommate, who'd once stayed on the air for twenty-seven straight hours during a blizzard because he believed the city needed rock and roll more than it needed sleep. Tom caught my eye and gave me the smallest nod that said: I know. Hang on.

"Let's talk about the future," Kowalski said.

He opened his portfolio and spread papers across the buckled table like a general deploying troops. Charts. Graphs. Demographic breakdowns printed in the kind of typeface that makes everything look scientific and nothing feel human. I could see columns of numbers, age ranges, household income brackets, pie charts sliced into segments labeled 18-24, 25-34, Male, Female, College-Educated, Blue-Collar.

"WBCN's core audience is aging," he said. "Our 25-34 demo is up seven percent, but our 18-24 — your growth market, your future — is down twelve percent in the last eighteen months. The advertisers who matter — automotive, audio equipment, lifestyle brands — they're buying 18-34. That's the sweet spot. That's where the dollars live."

He tapped a chart like a teacher correcting a student.

"We need to grow the 18-34 demo, or we lose the automotive sponsors. Lose the automotive sponsors, we lose the revenue that keeps this station independent. Lose the independence—" He spread his hands and smiled the kind of smile that knows it's winning. "Well. You all know what's happening to independent radio."

We did. Clear Channel was swallowing FM stations like a python digesting rabbits. One by one, independent voices replaced by automated playlists generated by consultants in offices that had never been within a thousand miles of the bands they programmed. Boston had lost three stations in two years. We all knew the python was circling our building.

Charlie tapped his pen on the table. "Gerald has a proposal."

Kowalski pulled out a single sheet. Clean. Typed. The heading read: WBCN COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT INITIATIVE — BATTLE OF THE BANDS.

"Regional high school music competition," he said. "WBCN sponsors. We brand it. We market it to schools within a thirty-mile radius of Boston. Kids enter their bands, we provide judges from our DJ roster, winner gets a recording session and airtime exposure. We sell sponsorship packages — Coca-Cola, local car dealerships, Jordan's Furniture — and position WBCN as the station that discovers the next generation of rock talent."

He paused. Looked around the table with the confidence of a man who knows he's selling something people are going to buy.

"It's community engagement that drives 18-34. It's authentic — local kids, local music, local pride. It's sponsorable — brands want to be associated with youth and discovery. And it's repeatable — we build it as an annual franchise that generates revenue every spring."

The silence in the room lasted about four seconds. The time it takes to cross a line you can't uncross.

"Annual franchise," Tom Andrews said. Not a question. A repetition, the way you repeat a diagnosis you're not ready to accept.

"The data supports it." Kowalski tapped his charts. "Stations that run community engagement programming see a fourteen percent lift in target demos within two rating periods. WJLB in Detroit. KROQ in LA. It's proven."

I looked at Tom. Tom looked at me. And in that look was everything we both understood: this was the moment. This was where the road forked. This was where WBCN either stayed what it was — a station that found real music and played it at full volume because we believed in it — or became what everything else was becoming. A brand.

I opened my mouth. And what came out surprised me.

"What if we use it to actually find talent?"

The table turned to me.

"Not as a brand exercise," I said. "Not as a demographic play. As what WBCN does. Discovery. We go into these schools and we listen. We send DJs who know the difference between a kid who can play and a kid who can make you feel something. We don't look for the next marketable act — we look for the next real thing. The next Aerosmith playing a bar in Allston that nobody knows about yet."

Tom leaned forward. "Maxanne's right. If we do this — if we put our name on it — it has to be authentic. WBCN discovers talent. That's the brand, Gerald. That's what we do. If this turns into a glorified corporate talent show, we lose the one thing that makes us worth sponsoring in the first place."

Kowalski watched us the way a chess player watches an opponent move exactly where he wants them. "I agree completely," he said.

He agreed. That should have been my first warning. When the man in the suit agrees with the rebels, it means the rebels just walked into the cage and closed the door behind themselves.

"Discovery. Authenticity. That's exactly the narrative we sell to sponsors. 'WBCN — Where Legends Begin.' We find talent, we give them a platform, sponsors associate their brands with the discovery process. Everybody wins."

Charlie tapped his pen. "So we're doing this?"

"We're doing this," Kowalski said. "First Battle — spring 1979. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School. I've already reached out to their music teacher, a Bob Wentworth, who's got connections to the local scene. He's enthusiastic. We start regional, prove the model, expand next year." He looked at me. "Maxanne, I want you to judge. You're the face of WBCN discovery. Your credibility makes this real."

My credibility. Like it was a product he could borrow.

"I'll judge," I said. "But I'm writing the rules."

Kowalski's smile didn't waver. "Of course. Tom, you co-draft with Maxanne. Get me something by Friday." He gathered his charts and his portfolio and his Italian shoes and stood. "One more thing. This needs to work. First time, every time. The sponsors are watching. Make it pay."

Make it pay.

He said it the way you'd tell a vending machine to deliver the soda after you've already put in the coins.

The door closed behind him and the room exhaled.

"Well," Charlie said, lighting a joint. "That's the future."

Tom and I sat in silence. The gold records on the wall stared down at us — bands we'd discovered when discovery meant something, when it wasn't a line item in a sponsorship deck.

"We can still make this real, right?" I said. Not to Tom. Not to Charlie. To the room itself, like the walls might answer.

Tom rubbed his eyes. "If we write the rules. If we control who judges. If we keep the sponsors at arm's length and the kids at the center."

"Then we write the rules," I said.

Nick and Jackie walked past each other in it like weather.

output:
73:"But first, we need to talk about a garage on Dutton Road, and why the ghost of a dead construction worker might have been the only adult who understood what was really at stake ... "
75:I close my eyes and let the memory take me back. May 1979. Warm enough that the windows in Grace Johnson's kitchen stood open, the peepers going out behind the Cavicchio fence, the last of the lilac in somebody's yard on Dutton Road. That's when I first drove out to Sudbury, following rumors about a kid who played guitar like he was trying to resurrect the dead.
82:Maxanne Sartori drove up to the Johnson house in her powder-blue Karmann Ghia, the car bottoming out twice on potholes the town never fixed on the working-class side of Hop Brook. Sparks kicked off the undercarriage. She didn't care. She'd heard rumors about a kid on Dutton Road—a kid with a voice that could stop you mid-dial-turn, playing in a garage where the sound punched you in the chest before you opened the door.
142:Walking back to the Karmann Ghia, she heard the music start again behind her. "Sweet Emotion"—that bass line crawling out of the garage and across the frozen yard like something that refused to stay buried. Four boys with nothing to lose. The sound carried across Dutton Road, past the potholed asphalt and the bare trees, toward Hop Brook, where it died against the far bank like every other signal that tried to cross from this side to the other.
412:Jackie would bring Queen albums recorded from his father's stereo system — bootleg copies of A Night at the Opera and News of the World dubbed onto TDK cassettes with handwritten labels in Jackie's careful block print. Nick would bring Aerosmith tapes borrowed from older kids on Dutton Road, the lyrics to "Dream On" and "Sweet Emotion" copied in ballpoint pen on notebook paper during study hall when he was supposed to be learning algebra.
438:Something in Jackie's careful manners — the way he held the plate with both hands, the way he waited until she took it — tugged at a memory Grace hadn't visited in years. Her own mother's dining room table, the good china reserved for Sunday dinners, the way her mother had stood behind her chair and guided her hands: napkin in the lap, elbows off the table, always say please and thank you. Her mother had grown up in a house with a name too, out in Wellesley, before she'd married a man who worked with his hands and moved to a street without sidewalks. Grace had learned her manners in a kitchen that smelled like lavender and lemon polish, and she'd carried them to a kitchen that smelled like dish soap and meatloaf and mortgage worry. She hadn't expected to recognize those same manners in a boy from Maple Street — but she did, and the recognition sat in her chest like a stone.
688:He thought about Nick Johnson. About that garage on Dutton Road where the concrete floor was cracked and the tools hung on pegboards and nobody measured the distance between anything. Where you could play as loud as you wanted and the only rule was that it had to be real.
702:The Johnson house on Dutton Road had crown molding in the dining room. Not the cheap pressed-foam kind you bought at the lumber yard — real plaster, hand-carved, with acanthus leaves that curled at the corners where the ceiling met the walls. Grace ran her fingers along the baseboard every time she vacuumed, the way you'd touch a scar without meaning to. Most of the molding was painted over now, three or four coats of landlord white, but if you looked where the living room met the front hall you could still see the original detail underneath — vines and small flowers cut into plaster by someone who'd been paid to make a house beautiful, back when this house was the kind of place where people got paid to do that.
850:Nick and Jackie had been playing together for almost two years by then. Garage sessions on Dutton Road, acoustic guitars and a keyboard Jackie hauled over on his bicycle, two years of arguing about whether Mercury or Tyler understood something deeper about what a voice could do. They were tight, and they were good, and nobody outside that garage knew it.
988:Dan drove the Johnsons home. Windows down, the May air carrying the smell of lilac from someone's yard on Dutton Road. Nick sat in the back seat holding his guitar case and the first-place ribbon and he couldn't stop talking — the riff, the moment the harmony locked, the look on Karen Bowers' face. Grace reached into the back seat and squeezed his knee, once, and let go. Dan watched the road and said nothing, but in the rearview mirror his eyes were bright.
1006:On Dutton Road, Nick lay on his bed with his hands behind his head, still hearing the sound. In the kitchen, Dan and Grace talked in low voices, and he could hear them laughing — Grace's high laugh and Dan's low one, two tones braiding the way two voices will when they've known each other long enough to harmonize without trying.
1371:That night, in the garage on Dutton Road, Jackie showed up with his guitar at six-thirty as if nothing had changed. Maybe for him nothing had. He tuned up, ran through a chord progression, waited for Nick to come in on top of it the way Nick always did.
1381:Jackie packed up his guitar and rode his bike home through the September dark, up Dutton Road toward the north side where the lawns got wider and the porch lights were the kind that turned on automatically at dusk. Nick stood in the garage doorway and watched the red reflector on Jackie's rear fender shrink until it was just a point of light and then nothing.
1391:Outside, September cooled toward October. The leaves on Dutton Road were just starting to turn, the green going pale at the edges, not yet the orange and red that would come but already not what they were — changing so slowly that if you watched them every day you'd swear nothing was different, and then one morning you'd look up and the whole street would be on fire and you'd wonder how you missed it.
1408:His loafers were polished. The bottoms of his jeans were an inch dark with Dutton Road mud because he had walked across the lawn yesterday to save thirty seconds. He noticed it now, the small pull of dried mud against the denim at every step.
1603:She made Dan's lunch the way she made it every morning. Tuna on white bread, the can opened and drained and mixed with mayonnaise and a little celery salt, the way her mother had made it for her father in this same kitchen when this had been her parents' house and the world had been a different shape. She spread the tuna with a butter knife, her hands moving without thought — hands that were forty-one years old and looked fifty, the knuckles swollen from hot water and fryer grease, the skin across the backs cracked in fine white lines like the glaze on old china. She wrapped the sandwich in wax paper, folded the edges tight, wrapped it again in aluminum foil. An apple. Two oatmeal cookies from Sunday night. Brown paper bag. Thermos.
1617:He walked down the driveway. The truck's headlights came on. The engine turned over, caught, settled. Red taillights moved down Dutton Road and disappeared where the road bent toward Route 20.
1805:The guitar spoke for him. The Dutton Road garage became his whole vocabulary. Sawdust and motor oil, the concrete slab cold enough through his socks to make your teeth ache, Dan's tools still on the pegboards in the exact order Dan left them — Phillips-heads in descending size, the coffee can of sixteen-penny nails, a wrench set nobody had moved since November. Nick played till his fingers bled through the calluses and then he played some more. He wasn't practicing. He was bleeding off pressure the only way he knew.
1886:The second Saturday in October, 1978. Eleven months since the trailer on Sixty State, near enough to a year that Nick had stopped counting and started rounding. The woods between Dutton Road and Cavicchio's back field were conservation land now, and the old stone walls ran through them waist-high, moss-headed, the farmers who'd stacked them a century gone and the sheep gone longer than that.
2091:That night, Nick stayed in the garage on Dutton Road past midnight with the tube amp humming and his left hand cramping around the neck of the Les Paul copy and the opening of "Dream On" under his fingers for the fortieth time — the way you grind a thing down until it either gives up its secret or breaks your hand. The concrete was cold through his sneakers. The pegboard on the wall was his father's. He did not stop.
2162:Nick drove the wood-paneled wagon home down Route 20 past the Store 24 where Dennis was working the four-to-midnight, and lifted two fingers off the steering wheel as he passed the window. The sun was low over the trees. The fields behind the Cavicchio place were still brown. He turned up Dutton Road. The Johnson house sat where it always sat, the white paint going gray on the north side, the bay window in the dining room catching the last of the light.
2210:Nick played it again. And again. The strings bit his fingertips. Outside, someone three houses down called a dog in for the night, and a truck on Route 20 downshifted for the light at Horse Pond Road, and the April dusk settled over Dutton Road the way it settled over every road in town — without asking, without promising anything.
2534:Grace set the receiver back in the cradle of the rotary phone on the kitchen wall, and the small internal click of the hanger-bar dropping into place was the last sound in the house. The kitchen clock ticked. Upstairs the garage amp was off. She stood with her hand still on the receiver for a second, then she turned off the kitchen light and went up the stairs in the dark the way she had gone up them ten thousand times, her right hand on the banister where the varnish had worn thin to the grain under her father's hand and her own.
2659:I'd already heard the rumors. Two kids from Sudbury — one working-class, one wealthy, once best friends, now enemies — both entering the Battle. Nick Johnson, the guitar kid from Dutton Road with the dead father's garage and the sound that could pull tears out of people who didn't know they were sad. Jackie Marsh, the classically trained prodigy from Maple Street with the Queen belt buckle and the rock and roll heart trapped inside a Juilliard application.
2723:She did not turn her head. She poured the regular. She said thank you to the Country Club man, who had not said anything to thank her for, and she walked back to the counter, past the ice cream case and the chalkboard and the hot-water jar that rang once again as the scoop went in, and she set the orange-collared pot on the warmer and lifted the brown-collared one off its plate. On the shelf under the register, next to the box of straws, the frosted glass jar of Maxwell House instant sat where it had sat every day she had worked here, and the shape of the jar — squat, shouldered, a little amber through the frost — was the shape of a jar a man had kept on the sideboard in a study on Dutton Road a long time ago, and for half a breath she was eight years old in a doorway watching him close the lid and label something and look up and smile before he remembered he was supposed to be working.
2941:The garage bay door stood up to the chest-high stop, lifted halfway for the air — the fourteenth of May in Sudbury, sixty-five degrees if it was a degree, the kind of spring night that felt warm only because April had set the bar so low. Crickets had started in the grass by the oil stain. Behind the Cavicchio fence a spring peeper was going in the wet low place, one note at a time, not fast. A Chevy with a bad belt whined down Dutton Road and faded toward the Horse Pond light.
2987:The laundry line ran from the porch post to the maple in the side yard and the line was empty — she had brought the sheets in at six the way she had brought them in every Thursday for twenty-three years. Across Dutton Road on the Connolly porch the orange cat sat on the railing with its tail hanging over the mailbox side. Up by the mill the Chevy with the bad belt passed again, coming back. The same one. The belt did the same thing.
2991:She was afraid of what he would do if he lost. She was afraid of what he would do if he won. Both fears were the same fear, and both fears had the same hand on the same chrome storm-door handle of the same house she had grown up in, on a step she had been standing on when the men from the District Attorney's office came up the walk in the late fall of '53 to ask her mother if she knew where her father kept his papers. She did not open the door. She stood with her hand on the handle until the chrome warmed. Then she took her hand off and went in.
3219:Dutton Road first. Nick's garage. His dead father's tools still on the pegboard in the exact order Dan left them — Phillips-heads in descending size, the coffee can of sixteen-penny nails, the wrench set nobody had moved since November of '77. Overhead bulb. Concrete cold through a pair of gym socks. An acoustic guitar worn raw at the twelfth fret because he won't stop playing it even when his fingers leave prints of blood on the strings.
3727:Dutton Road was quiet at a quarter to ten. Nick lay on top of his bedspread in his jeans and listened to the house tick the way houses did after everyone was supposed to be asleep. The refrigerator. A pipe in the wall. His mother's shoes coming off in the kitchen.
4008:Then Nick brought the talk-box line in without a talk-box. You couldn't buy a Heil for love or money on Dutton Road. He had worked the part out with the tone knob pulled halfway off and a borrowed wah held at the sweep-middle under his boot. He fingered the line on the D and G strings and rocked the toe of the boot in a slow quarter-inch arc, and what came out of the Twin was not a talk-box; it was a nasal rub, a close-mouthed vowel, the shape of Joe Perry's trick without Joe Perry's gear. It worked because it had to work.
4330:He turned up Dutton Road. The Johnson house sat where it always sat, white paint going gray on the north side, bay window dark, kitchen light on. Stephen put it in park.
4414:The amplifier hummed. A car passed on Dutton Road, headlights sweeping across the small window above the workbench and vanishing. Somewhere in the house a faucet ran and stopped.
4518:Grace drove. She did not ask questions. She had put a windbreaker on over the sweatshirt and she had taken her wallet because she was Grace Johnson and she did not leave the house at one in the morning without her wallet. The '67 wagon pulled out of Dutton Road onto Route 20 east and found the center line and stayed there. The speedometer sat at forty-five. The dash light was the color of old butter. Jackie had the Wurlitzer on his lap in the back seat with the cord wrapped around his wrist.
4567:Nick thought about the kitchen window, cracked two inches because the radiator made the room too hot in May. The sound of them playing carrying through the gap, across the yard, down Dutton Road. A frequency looking for a receiver.
4744:Dan would have understood. Dan had made his own bargain — his body for a paycheck, construction sites for a mortgage, physical labor for a house on Dutton Road where his son could play guitar in a garage that smelled like sawdust.
4768:He didn't mention Queen. He didn't mention the Crown Jewels, or the Battle of the Bands, or the Wurlitzer with the cracked middle C, or the garage on Dutton Road, or the studio at 3 AM. He said "classical" the way you close a door — firmly, with your back against it.

cd /workspace && git add -A && git commit -m "Draft 3.2 Wave 4: Grace-house canon fix + L-S as quadrant-crossing place-character

AUTHOR CORRECTION — Dutton Road is DAN'S family home, not Grace's.

Timothy clarified: the original implication that the Dutton Road
house was Grace's childhood home (reclaimed by her and Dan decades
later) was incorrect. Grace moved into the Johnson family home on
Dutton Road as a bride in 1956. Dan grew up there. Dan's father
bought it in the 1940s. Three generations of Johnson hands had worn
the banister before Grace's was the fourth. What happened to the
lost big house of Grace's childhood (on the north side of Hop Brook,
her father's house before the 1953 scandal) is insignificant to
the plot and deliberately left unspecified.

The emotional weight of Grace's widowhood now lands harder: she is
alone in Dan's ghost house, surrounded by the objects of his family
— not her own.

Fixes applied across the manuscript:

- Ch 12 'her mother had made it for her father in this same
  kitchen when this had been her parents' house' →
  'Dan's mother had made it for Dan's father in this same kitchen
  for forty years before Grace ever stood at this counter.'
  The tuna-sandwich lineage now flows through Dan's family.

- Ch 18 banister 'under her father's hand and her own' →
  'under three generations of Johnson hands and her own.'

- Ch 19 Maxwell-House jar father-hint moved from 'a sideboard in
  a study on Dutton Road' → 'a sideboard of a study in a big
  house on the other side of Hop Brook.' The jar was in her
  father's study in the lost house, not in her current house.

- Ch 21 chrome storm-door handle: 'the same chrome storm-door
  handle of the same house she had grown up in … the men from
  the District Attorney's office came up the walk in the late
  fall of '53' → 'the chrome storm-door handle of the house Dan
  had grown up in — the house she had walked into as a bride
  twenty-three years ago carrying a casserole and a suitcase, and
  had never walked out of since.' The 1953 DA's-office-at-the-walk
  beat (which belonged to the lost house, not this one) is
  removed from Ch 21. The Ch 18 library beat ('The Yearling' and
  the 1953 lemon-oil varnish) still holds — that's about L-S,
  not the Dutton Road house.

- _DRAFT_32_ADDENDUM.md updated with the full corrected backstory
  and the explicit manuscript fix-list.

SUDBURY QUADRANTS + L-S AS PLACE-CHARACTER.

Timothy requested the four quadrants be called out clearly and
that the high school (which sits in the 4th quadrant, southeast)
be treated as a main character. Ch 3 'The Geography of Sudbury'
already renders all four quadrants (northeast, northwest,
southwest, southeast) — but did not place Lincoln-Sudbury inside
the quadrant system. Added one new three-paragraph passage to
Ch 3 immediately before the final Hop Brook beat:

  'And then there was Lincoln-Sudbury itself. Set down in the
  southeast quarter in 1958 between Route 117 and Hop Brook's
  last loop before the Grist Mill, a brick and glass building
  that was the one address in town every quarter had to come

  auditorium at the center that held four hundred and forty-
  three folding seats — a building designed, whether anyone had
  meant to or not, to be the town's only real commons…'

  it and half-resented it. By 1979 it had been producing kids
  for twenty-one years.'

WORDS: 581
---SCENE---
STUDIO C, the door says, in stenciled letters older than anything the new tenant is planning to do with this frequency. The door is open. Four boxes are stacked in the hall beside it, labeled STUDIO C — EQUIPMENT in the same black marker that labeled everything else, as if the movers couldn't be bothered to distinguish a room from a room.

I have not been inside this room since May 16, 1979. Three twenty-five AM, give or take. I left it with a cardboard-sleeved reel under my arm and Grace Johnson idling in a station wagon in the lot and the two kids who made the tape standing in the doorway where I am standing now.

I stop. I do not go in.

Nine by twelve. I measured it once. Nine by twelve feet exactly, the smaller of the two demo studios in 1979 and a storage closet since the mid-nineties, which is what anybody will tell you if you ask. Nobody will tell you it was anything else.

The acoustic panels are piled in the far corner. Someone has unscrewed them from the walls for the move-out and stacked them the way you'd stack old mattresses, the quilted fabric going grey-brown where thirty years of dust have settled into the weave. On the walls they left behind is the original 1968 plaster, the color of old butter, and on the plaster are the clean shadow-rectangles where each panel used to sit. Clean patches on dirty plaster, the shapes of things that used to matter.

The Yamaha U3 is gone. Sold at auction in '91 or '92 — an engineer told me once at a wrap party, offhand, the way you mention the weather. On the linoleum where it sat there are four small rectangular marks in the floor, one at each leg, pressed into the tile by the piano's own weight over twenty-three years. Four small rectangles in a pattern I could draw in my sleep.

I look at them.

I do not cry. I do not make a sound. I close my eyes for two beats and open them, and the room stays what it is — a storage closet with its storage stripped, a piano-shaped ghost on the floor, a folding chair nobody put away.

The chair sits facing the doorway. Aluminum, the kind the custodian used to drag in when a third person came to a session. Somebody took a break here and did not come back for it.

The boom stands are gone. The DI box off the floor is gone. The control-room glass past the panels is still there, smudged, the control room beyond it stripped to bare conduit.

For three seconds I let myself have it. The D minor chord Jackie's hands found on the Yamaha at two-fourteen AM, thirty years and seventeen weeks ago. Just the one chord. Not the whole song. My memory has always let me have it and has never let me have more.

A janitor passes me in the hall with a mop bucket, younger than my daughter would have been if I'd had one, the casters squeaking on the linoleum. "You doing okay, ma'am." He does not stop.

"Fine. Thank you."

He does not stop.

I stand another beat in the doorway. One step and I am across the sill. I do not take it. Crossing the sill tonight would break something I am not prepared to break. The broadcast is still to come.

I keep walking.

Cleaning a kitchen that did not need cleaning was one of the two or three actions available to a woman of her age and her street when something had to be done and could not be named, and she had put the other two down a long time ago.
