+
+From the study, the faint sound of Richard's pencil against a stack of BU undergraduate papers, the small periodic tap when he squared a sheet on the desk. He would be at them until eleven-thirty.
+
+Three notes of a Brahms lieder she had not opened her mouth for in public since a Tuesday afternoon in the fall of 1953 came up unasked, from a shelf lower in her throat than she used now. Contralto low. The register she had trained in before her voice had ever been called a voice. She hummed them. Just the three. Her hand at the base of the cookie jar stopped. She held the three notes in her throat the way a person holds a breath underwater, a small bright pressure behind the sternum — and then she caught herself, and the notes ended, and her hand on the cloth began to move again, harder this time, a tight small circle. The cloth was soaked. Water ran down her wrist to the inside of her forearm and she did not notice it.
+
+On the upper shelf of the pantry, behind the two-tier line of Hunt's tomato cans she kept against winter, was a small flat box wrapped in brown paper and tied with butcher's string. She did not look up at it. She knew where it was the way she knew where the silver was.
+
+She wrung the cloth out in the sink. It came out gray. She filled the copper kettle at the tap, set it on the front burner, and turned the gas to medium. It caught with its small blue sigh.
+
+Upstairs the measure went by again — not stopped this time, carried through — and the line of the Nocturne moved on into its second phrase and was gone around the bend of the melody.
+
+The kettle whistled. She made the tea in the Spode cup her mother-in-law had given her in 1958. She carried the cup through the dining room and into the living room and set it on the side table beside her armchair. The Patrick Leigh Fermor was open face-down on the cushion where she had left it Sunday. *A Time to Keep Silence.* Page one hundred twenty-four. She had been on that page for three weeks.

II.
JACKIE
August 1979 — Manhattan

The room was nine feet by eleven. Jackie knew because he'd measured it. A twin bed, a desk, a dresser, a window that looked onto West 66th Street where taxis moved in yellow procession and the sound never stopped. His bedroom in Sudbury had been fourteen by sixteen with a view of the oak tree his mother had planted the year he was born.

...

Then the weight came down and the C sounded, clean and warm, the exact C of a Steinway Model B on a fourth-floor afternoon in mid-February, and his left hand came up to meet it, and *Des pas sur la neige* began the way it always began — slow, the tread of a figure over snow. He played it through. He played it perfectly. He played it with care and precision and no visible effort. The last pianissimo settled into the pedal and he held it the length Debussy asked for and he lifted his foot.

He closed the lid. He gathered the sheet music. He walked out. In the hallway the cellist had moved on to a different passage. Somebody at the far end was laughing again.

---

III.
MAXANNE
1982 and after

The Elektra office on Columbus Avenue had a window that looked at another window. Brick across an airshaft. Pigeons on the sill of the building opposite. A view that taught you to keep your eyes on your desk.

Fall of '82. Five years out of WBCN. Three years out from the Battle. She'd stopped counting months by then and started counting in albums — the ones she'd signed, the ones she'd lost, the ones she'd fought for in budget meetings and watched get killed by men in better suits than hers. The refusal to compromise that had made her Maxanne at the station was, at Elektra, slower to kill her but just as thorough.

She'd kept the office sparse. A promo poster for the first album she'd championed, already curling at the corner. A Sony dictation machine. A Rolodex thick with phone numbers of people who owed her favors, and a smaller one with the numbers of people she owed. The locked drawer was bottom right.

cd /workspace && python3 <<'PY'
import re, pathlib
MANU = pathlib.Path("Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_1_Complete.txt")
lines = MANU.read_text().split("\n")

def find_chapter_range(lines, ch_label):
    pat_ch = re.compile(rf"^(# |## )?CHAPTER {re.escape(ch_label)}(\b|:|\s|—|$)")
    pat_next = re.compile(r"^(# |## )?CHAPTER \d+[A-Z]?(\b|:|\s|—|$)")
    start = None
    for i, ln in enumerate(lines):
        if pat_ch.match(ln.strip()) and not re.match(rf"^(# |## )?CHAPTER {re.escape(ch_label)}[A-Z]", ln.strip()):
            start = i; break
    if start is None: return None
    end = len(lines)
    for j in range(start+1, len(lines)):
        if pat_next.match(lines[j].strip()):
            end = j; break
    return start, end

# Integrate in reverse order so earlier indices don't shift
for ch in ["9A", "2", "1"]:
    rng = find_chapter_range(lines, ch)
    if not rng: print(f"Ch {ch}: NOT FOUND"); continue
    start, end = rng
    filename = f"ch0{ch}_rewrite.txt" if ch in ("1","2") else "ch09A_rewrite.txt"
    rewrite = pathlib.Path(f"Draft_3/scalpel_hose_rewrites/{filename}").read_text().rstrip("\n")
    new_block = rewrite.split("\n") + ["", ""]
    print(f"Ch {ch}: replace {end-start} lines with {len(new_block)}; header={lines[start]!r}")
    lines[start:end] = new_block

MANU.write_text("\n".join(lines))
PY
echo "---manuscript wc---"
wc -w Draft_3/Walk_This_Way_Draft_3_1_Complete.txt

436:The first time Jackie came to dinner at the Johnson house, Grace watched him from the kitchen doorway. She'd heard about the Marsh family from the other mothers — the psychiatrist at Boston University, the house on Maple Street, the kind of people who didn't usually sit at tables with mismatched chairs and bills spread on the counter.
440:Something in Jackie's careful manners — the way he held the plate with both hands, the way he waited until she took it — tugged at a memory Grace hadn't visited in years. Her own mother's dining room table, the good china reserved for Sunday dinners, the way her mother had stood behind her chair and guided her hands: napkin in the lap, elbows off the table, always say please and thank you. Her mother had grown up in a house with a name too, out in Wellesley, before she'd married a man who worked with his hands and moved to a street without sidewalks. Grace had learned her manners in a kitchen that smelled like lavender and lemon polish, and she'd carried them to a kitchen that smelled like dish soap and meatloaf and mortgage worry. She hadn't expected to recognize those same manners in a boy from Maple Street — but she did, and the recognition sat in her chest like a stone.
468:"Sure looks like it. Professor daddy, house on Maple Street. What are you doing over here?"
482:Doug looked from Nick to Jackie and back. He was trying to do the math — working-class kid defending a kid from Maple Street — and the numbers didn't add up.
2218:The Howard Miller grandfather clock in the hall struck six-thirty and the Marshes sat. That was how it worked on Maple Street — the clock began to strike, and by the fourth tone the four of them were at the table with napkins across their laps. The tick kept going after the chime. Seventy-two to the minute. Andante.
2310:Jackie looked past her at the window. Maple Street at dusk. The streetlights were coming on in sequence — the Caldwells', then the Petersons', then the Schiffs', each one striking a second behind the last, a small orderly arpeggio of sodium glow down a row of hedges clipped to the same height. Someone was pulling into a driveway in a Buick the color of a Buick.
2330:She thought about it. She thought about it a long time. The clock downstairs kept its andante. The sodium lamps on Maple Street came on in their order.
2682:I'd already heard the rumors. Two kids from Sudbury — one working-class, one wealthy, once best friends, now enemies — both entering the Battle. Nick Johnson, the guitar kid from Dutton Road with the dead father's garage and the sound that could pull tears out of people who didn't know they were sad. Jackie Marsh, the classically trained prodigy from Maple Street with the Queen belt buckle and the rock and roll heart trapped inside a Juilliard application.
3051:May 14, 1979. Early evening. Eighteen hours to the Battle and Jackie Marsh was alone in the basement on Maple Street, running the intro of "Bohemian Rhapsody" in B-flat because his left hand had asked for it the second he sat down.
3776:Two miles north, on Maple Street, Dr. Richard Marsh's house faced a row of hedges clipped to the same height every April by the same man. Jackie's bedroom was on the third floor, under the eaves. The Steinway was two floors below him and might as well have been in another country.

272:And then there was Lincoln-Sudbury itself. Set down in the southeast quarter in 1958 between Route 117 and Hop Brook's last loop before the Grist Mill, a brick and glass building that was the one address in town every quarter had to come to. The Cavicchio kids walked to it. The northwest kids got driven in waxed station wagons. The northeast kids rode the '75 bus from the end of Dutton Road, and the southwest kids rolled up in Volvos with college-alumni stickers on the rear window. The school did not care which door you came in. It had four of them, one on each face, and a proscenium auditorium at the center that held four hundred and forty-three folding seats — a building designed, whether anyone had meant to or not, to be the town's only real commons. Every kid in Sudbury between fourteen and eighteen was in that building thirty-five hours a week for four years. The cafeteria was where the four quarters sorted themselves back into the cliques they recognized. The Glass Corridor was where the ones who refused to be sorted smoked Lucky Strikes in the 1979 fashion. The auto shop bay opened onto the back parking lot where the Rollers rebuilt what their fathers could not afford to replace. And the music wing, two doors past the gym, was where the whole mess of it occasionally found a tune.

1712:Three guitar picks. Fender mediums, tortoiseshell, worn smooth at the edges from use. A stack of sheet music — not store-bought but handwritten on staff paper in Dan's careful block print, the notes drawn with the same precision he used on blueprints. "Stairway to Heaven." "Wish You Were Here." "Landslide." Chords marked in pencil, fingering notes in the margins — barre chord here, capo third fret, hammer-on to the suspended fourth.
3357:"I want to play our songs. 'Dreams.' 'Landslide.' 'Silver Springs.' 'Go Your Own Way.' The way we play them — not louder, not angrier, not more perfect. Just honest."
3487:"Landslide" second. Slow it down. Make them listen.
3497:"Landslide" said: Time passes. You can't stop it. What matters is what survives.
3521:"Landslide" came next. Patty alone at first — just voice and acoustic, the pick pattern Stevie Nicks had turned into a kind of lullaby for grown-ups. The church went still. Even Steve put his sticks down. There was no percussion in "Landslide," and Steve was smart enough to know that silence was a drummer's most powerful tool.
3659:She could stand on that stage and play music that didn't ask for anything — not victory, not vindication, not proof that one kind of life was worth more than another. She could play "Dreams" and mean it. She could play "Landslide" and let her voice crack on the second line because the crack was real and real was the whole point. She could play "Silver Springs" and let the chorus swell until the walls pushed back. She could close with "Go Your Own Way" and let the room decide what that meant — separation or invitation, goodbye or open door.

Robin came up on her left with the bass. Kristy took the Fender and the second mic. Steve Bankuti was already behind the kit, a kid from Sudbury Southeast whose father drove a milk route; he adjusted his snare stand one quarter-turn and then sat with his sticks crossed on his knee like a boy waiting to be told he was allowed to stand up at the dinner table.

Patty leaned into the mic. She did not say anything. She tuned her B string — B was always the one — and she nodded at Robin.

In the wings stage-left Nick was leaning on a flight case with a towel around his neck. In the wings stage-right, across the width of the proscenium, Jackie was standing the way Jackie stood when he was trying not to be seen, hands at his sides, the black piano jacket still buttoned. Patty saw both of them the way you see a thing you are not going to look at twice. She looked back at the neck of the guitar.

Steve's kick pedal squeaked on beat two. A small high squeak, a dry hinge, the way his father's truck door squeaked. Patty smiled — a small unmeant smile, because something had surprised her — and went into the opening figure of "Dreams."

*Now here you go again, you say you want your freedom.*

She held the word *go*. Not long, the way a singer shows off a hold, but long enough. Her C chord rang out clean under it, the one she had botched in the empty St. Michael's on Monday night and laughed at out loud — her ring finger sat in the third fret now and did not buzz. The auditorium came down off the high Aerosmith ride it had been on. A JV booster-club mother halfway down the aisle with a cardboard tray of Cokes stopped mid-stride between booths and did not put the tray down; she only stopped. In row H a man put his arm around his wife's shoulder and left it there. The held note came down onto the next line and Patty let it.

She did not talk between songs. She tuned the B again. Robin adjusted a tuning peg. Kristy sipped water. Steve wiped his palms on his jeans. The room waited the way a room waits when it has agreed, without anyone saying so, that the person on the stage gets to choose the pace.

She counted them in for "Silver Springs."

This one she had not learned for Nick and Jackie. She had learned it last week in the fluorescent-lit basement of St. Michael's from a cassette Kristy had dubbed, and she had sung it out loud to four middle-aged parish women who came on Thursdays to arrange the altar flowers, and those four women had stood in the doorway of the basement with their hands in their cardigan pockets and listened. Her grandmother had sung in a kitchen in Sudbury Southeast to a radio on top of a Frigidaire in 1954. Her mother had sung in the same kitchen in 1966 with a baby on her hip. When Patty came into the long held second chorus — *you'll never get away from the sound of the woman that loves you* — she was not thinking about Nick. She was not thinking about Jackie. She was thinking about the four women at St. Michael's and the two women in her kitchen, and the private inheritance that lived in her hands was what went out into the microphone. The note bloomed. Kristy came in on the second *loves you* with a harmony a third below, and the two voices braided and held, and Steve's ride cymbal shimmered under it like water moving over flat stones.

The man in row H had his face in his hand. Patty could see him because the house lights were half up, the way Lincoln-Sudbury ran the Battle so the judges could take notes; she could see the whole first fifteen rows as clearly as she could see her own fingers. She let the chorus fall and stepped back off the mic and tuned the B one more time.

Robin looked at her. Patty nodded.

Steve's count-in on the sticks was a count-in she had been hearing in her head since sometime last November — four clean clicks of maple on maple — and then the bass came in on the Lindsey Buckingham pulse, eighth notes driving, and Kristy's rhythm guitar chunked down on the one, and Patty opened her mouth and sang the song that had been living under her breath since the jazz band room.

4989:CHAPTER 34: THE LAST VOICE OF BOSTON ROCK — PART 2
*It is BLOWING UP.*

I open the laptop on the passenger seat. The WBCN WiFi still works because nobody's thought to kill it yet. YouTube loads in the blue glow.

TWO GUYS WHO SHOULD HAVE BEEN FAMOUS — WBCN FINAL BROADCAST. Posted fourteen minutes ago by BostonRockRIP. Thumbnail of the antenna tower in Impact font.

50,000 views.

I refresh. 78,000.

The comments scroll past the way the request line used to scroll at eleven on a Friday night.

*1979??? This sounds like it could be today.*

*Who are these kids and how do I find them.*

*Sitting in my car in the parking lot of a CVS in Quincy crying.*

*Aerosmith plus Queen = this. How is this not a record.*

*Whoever played this on her last broadcast is a legend.*

*The Neighborhoods opened for the Cars at the Rat in '79 and these guys never even made the card. This is criminal.*

*RIP WBCN. Thank you Maxanne.*

I refresh. 140,000. 212,000. Twelve-thirty, three hundred thousand. The number climbs like something alive.

My phone rings. 212. New York. I don't answer. It rings again. 617. I don't answer. 310. Los Angeles. The calls stack up the way planes stack over Logan in weather. A voicemail from a producer at NPR. A voicemail from a writer at Pitchfork. A text from Carter Alan: *Maxanne what did you do.* A text from a number I don't know: *do you know where they are.*

One million views at 1:14 AM.

I am crying. Not sadness, not happiness. Some older thing my face knew before I did.

I close the laptop. The car goes black. I sit there in the Volvo in the empty lot with my hands on the wheel and I let myself think what I have not let myself think for thirty years.

---

Somewhere in a practice room on Mass Ave, on a Wednesday afternoon a month from now, a man in his late forties will be sitting at a Steinway Model B. Not his own Steinway. His office feels wrong today and he has been drifting through practice rooms since noon, the way he has been drifting through them more and more often this year without quite admitting to himself that he is. The teaching day is mostly over. His last two students canceled — one by email, one by not showing up. The room is provisionally his, the way an academic room is provisionally anyone's: forty minutes, then somebody else's. The lid is open on the full stick. He is not playing. He has not played seriously for himself in years. He plays *for* students now — demonstrates voice leading at the keyboard, voices a chord to make a point, closes the lid at the hour.

He is sitting with his hands resting on his thighs. His back is straight. His feet are flat under the pedals. It is the shape his body settled into one February afternoon in a practice room on West 66th Street thirty years ago, and it is a shape his body has been returning to more and more these last years, Wednesdays like this one, hands quiet on the wool of his slacks, the piano warm and unplayed in front of him. He has not yet noticed. He will notice, someday.

Someone will come to the door with a laptop. A colleague, maybe, or a kid from the theory class — somebody young enough to have found it first. They will say, you have to hear this. He will not move at first. He will listen all the way through, four minutes and forty-three seconds, with his hands in his lap and his eyes closed. And when it ends his right hand will lift from his thigh. It will not lift because he lifts it. It will lift the way a hand lifts from a table when someone calls you from the next room and you are already rising before you have decided. It will move across the air over the keys and come down on the D above middle C without pressing — the pad of the finger resting on the ivory, the key not moving, the string not sounding. A beat. Two beats. Then his left hand will come up to meet it. The weight will come down. The D minor chord will sound, just the chord, just once — and he will nod, very slightly, the way people nod when they finally hear somebody say out loud the thing they had decided they were alone with.

I don't know him. I have never met him. I am making him up in a Volvo in an empty parking lot at one-twenty in the morning because I need to. He might be out there. He might not. The imagining is what I have.

I turn the key. The Volvo catches on the second try. I drive out onto the Pike heading west, toward Cambridge, toward home, and I leave the radio off.

**END CHAPTER 34**

1527:Across from Jackie, Donnie Rossi was eating a meatball sub. Three sports this year — soccer, basketball, baseball — and the knuckle-scrape on his right hand from a headfirst slide on Feeley's mud Wednesday. The sub came from his uncle's deli off Concord Road, wrapped in white butcher paper saturated with sauce and sitting on an open section of the *Boston Globe* sports page so the sauce wouldn't stain the formica. Donnie did everything fast. His dress shirt had been ironed on Sunday night by a mother who woke at five-thirty six days a week to work the breakfast shift at the Friendly's on Route 20, and by Friday the shirt was a different object from the one that had come off the board — cuff-rolled, collar limp, a stripe of sauce at the second button.
3827:May 15, 1979. Seven o'clock on a Tuesday night. The Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium had been built in 1958 and smelled like it still — wood floor wax, the slow mineral breath of cast iron, four hundred and forty-three folding seats bolted into a concrete rake that groaned as kids sat down and groaned again when kids stood back up to wave at other kids. The fluorescent cove lights above the proscenium threw the whole room into the color of a grocery store. Behind the stage hung the painted backdrop every school play had used for a decade: a Concord Road maple tree in October, the red gone brown at the edges where the scrim had rolled. In the lobby the JV booster club had set up a popcorn machine and the smell of commercial butter and Aqua Velva and girls' perfume had come in with the crowd and was now layered, impossibly, on top of the baseline adolescent sweat of an April-warm room in May. The balcony was already full. Seniors.
